AND NOW, May 20, 2014, pursuant to the Fiscal Code, the Act of 1929, April 9, P.L. 343,
as amended, (72 P.S. § 1 et seq), the Board of Finance and Revenue of the Commonwealth of
Pennsylvania, based upon the reasons set forth herein, hereby ORDERS the following:
Jurisdiction
This petition comes before the Board of Finance and Revenue pursuant to Section 2704
of the Tax Reform Code, as amended, 72 P.S. § 9704.
Issue
Whether Petitioner is entitled to a refund for tax paid on receipts that it claims were not
received from providing “mobile telecommunications services messages.”
Statement of the Case
Petitioner, Commonwealth Telephone Company, LLC, originally filed its 2009 Gross
Receipts Tax return reporting $ in intrastate gross receipts and an intrastate gross
receipts tax liability of $ .
The Department reviewed the return and increased Petitioner’s taxable intrastate gross
receipts to $ . The Department assessed Petitioner additional intrastate gross
receipts tax in the amount of $ in an assessment notice issued on October 19, 2011.
Petitioner filed a Petition for Refund at the Board of Appeals (“BOA”) on September 5,
2013, claiming that tax was paid on receipts that were not subject to the gross receipts tax. In
its Decision and Order dated September 5, 2013, the BOA found that directory advertising

revenues were not related to the transmission of messages, and removed $ from the
taxable gross receipts. Petitioner’s tax liability was reduced to $ , and the BOA
denied all other claims. The additional tax liability resulting from the assessment was satisfied
through payment and/or credit transfer.
Petitioner files the instant matter at the Board of Finance and Revenue arguing that it is
entitled to exclude receipts that were not received from providing intrastate telephone
messages services from its taxable gross receipts, including: Universal Service Fund receipts,
wire maintenance fees, and customer premise equipment.
Petitioner argues that during the period at issue it earned receipts from fees for
maintenance services. Petitioner states the fees earned from the maintenance services are
solely for labor costs incurred in repairing technical problems that its customers had. Petitioner
argues that a recent court decision in Verizon v. Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, 72 A.3d 799
(Pa. Commw. 2013), analyzed repairs of telephone equipment. Petitioner states that in
Verizon, the Court held that no telephone messages are transmitted when Verizon performed
its repair services. Petitioner argues that in doing so, the Court in Verizon upheld the Dauphin
County Common Pleas Court’s decision in Commonwealth v. The Bell Telephone Company of
Pennsylvania, 14 Pa. D. & C. 675 (1930) (Bell II), which also held that “work done by Bell’s
employees that included custom work and installation of Bell’s own equipment or service” was
not taxable. Verizon, 72 A3.d at 802-803 (citing Bell II, 14 Pa. D. & C. at 681).
Petitioner argues that like Verizon, it sends employees to customer locations in order to
perform maintenance and service repair services. Its customers receive an invoice for the
service charges incurred. Accordingly, under Verizon, Petitioner argues that its receipts from
wire maintenance services must be treated as nontaxable.
Next, Petitioner argues that receipts from revenue attributable to customer premise
equipment are not attributable to “telegraph or telephone messages transmitted wholly within
this State…” as required by 72 P.S. § 8101(a)(2). Petitioner states these receipts are largely
attributable
Petitioner states that these types of receipts were also addressed by the court in
Verizon in a reference to Bell II, which it states held that receipts from charges for materials
and appliances furnished, “including sale of new materials and sale of old materials….is not
taxable for gross receipts.” 14 Pa. D. & C. 682.
Petitioner argues that Bell II is still controlling law with respect to these types of receipts.
Petitioner states that Bell II defined the term “traffic” to mean the “transmission of messages”
which, as Verizon noted, is the same language that has been used in analyzing the current
“telegraph or telephone messages transmitted” language. Verizon, 72 A.3d at 806. Petitioner
argues that no transmission of a message has occurred in connection with its receipts from
customer premise equipment, and accordingly are not subject to tax.
Finally, Petitioner argues that the assessed receipts attributable to Universal Service
Fund (“USF”) represents revenue that it collects from its customers which is in turn contributed
to the Federal USF fund. Petitioner states that these charges are mandated by the FCC, and

Petitioner also argues that the tax imposed violates various provisions of the United

Statement of the Law
General Rule.— Every . . . telephone company, telegraph company or provider of
mobile telecommunications services now or hereafter incorporated or organized by or under
any law of this Commonwealth, or now or hereafter organized or incorporated by any other
state or by the United States or any foreign government and doing business in this
Commonwealth, and every limited partnership, association, joint-stock association,
copartnership, person or persons, engaged in telephone or telegraph business or providing
mobile telecommunications services in this Commonwealth, shall pay to the State Treasurer,
through the Department of Revenue, a tax of forty-five mills with a surtax equal to five mills
upon each dollar of the gross receipts of the corporation, company or association, limited
partnership, joint-stock association, copartnership, person or persons, received from:
. . . .
(2) telegraph or telephone messages transmitted wholly within this State and
telegraph or telephone messages transmitted in interstate commerce where such
messages originate or terminate in this State and the charges for such messages
are billed to a service address in this State, except gross receipts derived from:
(i) the sales of access to the Internet, as set forth in Article II, made
to the ultimate consumer; and
(ii) the sales for resale to persons, partnerships, associations,
corporations or political subdivisions subject to the tax imposed by
this article upon gross receipts derived from such resale of
telecommunications services, including:
(A) telecommunications exchange access to
interconnect with a local exchange carrier's network;
(B) network elements on an unbundled basis; and

Revenue derived from a telephone subscriber for the use of facilities making telephone
communication more satisfactory must be regarded as being a part of the charge for
transmission of the messages. Commonwealth v. Bell Tel. Co., 348 Pa. 161 (Pa. 1943), at
166.
Except as otherwise provided by this act, in all cases of petitions filed pursuant to this
article, the burden of proof shall be upon the petitioner or appellant, as the case may be.
72 P.S. § 9705.
Every petition . . . filed with the Board shall set forth the facts and points of law on which
the petitioner relies. Any evidence in support of the petition shall be submitted simultaneously
with the petition or as promptly as possible thereafter. All evidential material shall be
submitted prior to five working days of the hearing date. 61 Pa. Code § 701.3(c).
Conclusion
Petitioner’s request for relief was correctly denied because Petitioner has not provided
sufficient details and evidence in support of its claims. See 72 P.S. § 9705 (imposing the
burden of proof on taxpayers in administrative tax appeals); see also 61 Pa. Code § 701.3(c)
(requiring specific objections supported by legal authority and evidence).
Petitioner has not shown that universal fund receipts, wire maintenance fees, and customer
premise equipment were not derived from providing intrastate telephone messages services. As
these services were related to the transmission of messages, these receipts are properly included in
Petitioner’s taxable gross receipts. See Bell Tel., 348 Pa. at 166 (finding that revenue telephone
companies derive from a customer for the use of services making telephone communication more
satisfactory are part of the charge for transmission of the messages).
As to Petitioner’s challenge to the validity and/or constitutionality of the statutes at issue,
the Board of Finance and Revenue can only apply the current state of Pennsylvania law and
cannot pass upon the validity or constitutionality of that law. See Parsowith v. Commonwealth
of Pennsylvania Department of Revenue, 555 Pa. 200, 723 A.2d 659 (1999); Land Holding
Corp. v. Board of Finance and Revenue, 388 Pa. 61, 130 A.2d 700 (1957).
Accordingly, Petitioner’s request for relief is hereby denied.
